transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-04-10
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~60 minutes
Attendees: Maya Cho (Redwood AE), Liam Patel (Redwood SE), Alicia Ramos (CISO - NorthernCrest), Devon Lee (Head of Cloud Infra), Marcus Ng (Security Engineer)

Summary: Deep dive on private deployment options for Redwood Private / VPC and on-prem integrations. Focus on network isolation, ingress/egress controls, firewalling, KMS/HSM key management, audit logs, SOC2/ISO evidence, SSO/RBAC and SIEM forwarding. Customer has strict egress rules and prefers customer-managed KMS.

Topics: private VPC architecture, bastion/jumpbox, peering vs transit, egress NAT/proxy, firewall rules/security groups/NACLs, mutual TLS for control plane, HSM integration, audit log forwarding to Splunk, SOC2/ISO questions, RBAC via SAML/SCIM.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya, account lead on Redwood. Liam is our solutions engineer, he'll drive the architecture details. Alicia: thanks.
[02:05] Liam: cool, quick agenda — confirm your constraints, walk through our typical private VPC architecture, then deep dive on ingress/egress and KMS/HSM options, and finish with next steps. Does that work?
[04:33] Alicia: yes, thanks. high level — NorthernCrest is moving inference into a private environment. Key requirements: no internet-facing inference nodes, KMS customer-managed keys, audit logs forwarded to our Splunk instance, SOC2 + ISO evidence for vendor, and fine-grained RBAC integrated with our SSO. Timeline: want pilot in Q2.
[05:30] Liam: got it — typical. One clarification, when you say no internet-facing nodes, do you mean no public IPs at all and egress only through approved proxies?
[06:10] Devon: correct, no public IPs. Egress must go through our outbound proxy and be whitelisted. We also prefer VPC peering over internet-facing endpoints, and ideally use a transit gateway for multi-account setup.
[08:00] Maya: perfect, Redwood Private supports VPC-only deployments. Our control plane can be run as a private control plane in your VPC, or we can run a managed control plane with private peering — depends on compliance. Liam will explain the two patterns.
[09:20] Liam: pattern A: customer-managed control plane (on-prem or in customer account) — full network isolation, we provide the software package or helm charts; pattern B: Redwood-managed control plane with VPC peering and no public egress — uses private endpoints and strict mTLS. Both support customer KMS.
[11:05] Marcus: for KMS — we need AES-256 keys in our HSM, rotation policies, and key usage audit. Do you support external HSM or key-wrapping?
[12:40] Liam: yes — two options: 1) Customer-managed KMS/HSM where Redwood services call your KMS via IAM role and CMK; 2) Bring-your-own-key with envelope encryption where we hold wrapped keys. For HSM we support PKCS#11 integrations and can integrate with cloud HSMs (AWS CloudHSM) or on-prem HSMs over a secure VPN/peering. There is some setup work for network egress to the KMS endpoint.
[14:30] Alicia: what's the network path for KMS calls with customer-managed KMS? We need those calls to stay on private network/VPC endpoints.
[15:10] Liam: we use VPC endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) or direct connect peering so KMS calls remain on the private backbone. If using customer KMS in the same account, calls never hit the public internet. For cross-account/ on-prem we recommend a private connection (Direct Connect or VPN) to avoid egress to the internet.
[17:00] Devon: ok, about ingress: how do we bootstrap, are there any temporary public access steps? We have strict change control and can't allow temporary open windows except via a jumpbox.
[18:25] Liam: bootstrap is flexible — we support an admin bastion/jumpbox pattern. You can use a temporary jumpbox with ephemeral keys, or use a secure file transfer for certs. We also support SSO-based admin flows so no long-lived passworded accounts are required.
[20:00] Marcus: what about firewalling and security groups? We have NACLs at the subnet level and stateful security groups. We want full list of ports and CIDR ranges to allow.
[21:15] Liam: we'll provide a definitive port list, but high level: control plane API ports (HTTPS 443) for private endpoints, internal gRPC between inference nodes on ephemeral ports, and admin SSH only to bastion. Egress to KMS, S3 for model artifacts, and your SIEM endpoint for logs. CIDR ranges are configurable per deployment. We'll share a spreadsheet with port/role mapping.
[23:40] Alicia: audit logs — we require immutable logs sent to our Splunk for 7 years, and we need tamper-evidence. How do you do audit logging?
[24:55] Liam: logs can be forwarded to your SIEM via syslog or S3 bucket with bucket policies preventing deletion by Redwood. We can sign logs and include cryptographic hashes for tamper evidence. Retention is customer-configurable; we can write directly to your encrypted S3 bucket and you manage lifecycle policies.
[26:30] Devon: do you support streaming audit logs in near-real-time? We need sub-minute ingestion for certain alerts.
[27:05] Liam: yes, we can stream via Kinesis or direct syslog to your splunk forwarder; latency is typically under 30 seconds depending on network. We'll test during pilot to confirm.
[29:10] Marcus: encryption at rest — are models and KV cache encrypted with our CMKs?
[30:00] Liam: yes, encryption at rest for model artifacts, snapshots, and KV cache can be configured to use customer CMKs. For ephemeral in-memory cache, data is in RAM and not persisted, but swap and dump protections apply. We'll document memory protections and secure disposal.
[31:10] Alicia: regulatory question — do you have SOC2 Type II and ISO27001? We need evidence as part of vendor onboarding.
[32:05] Maya: yes, we have SOC2 Type II and ISO27001. I'll share the current reports and a redacted pen test summary. For legal we also provide audit contact for any deeper SOC queries. (brief pause) Note: we'll share via secure link.
[33:40] Marcus: any public pen test reports? We do periodic internal pen tests and want to compare scope.
[34:20] Maya: we can share an executive summary and scope; full reports require an NDA in some cases. I'll include the steps to request the full report.
[36:00] Devon: network egress controls — if we allow only outbound to our proxy, how do you handle software updates/patches or container image pulls?
[37:30] Liam: two approaches: 1) cached artifact repository inside your VPC — you mirror Redwood images and updates; or 2) allow a very small outbound egress to Redwood's artifact endpoint over TLS and restrict to specific FQDNs/IPs with mutual TLS. For strict customers we always recommend mirroring images to a private repo.
[39:20] Alicia: how do you verify supply chain/attestation? We need SBOM and image signing for inference runtime.
[40:05] Liam: we provide signed images and an SBOM for the runtime components. We support image signing with Sigstore (or cosign) and can provide attestations that can be validated during your CI/CD gating.
[41:40] Marcus: what about RBAC and SSO? We use SAML 2.0 and SCIM for group provisioning. Need per-route audit and role-based restrictions.
[42:20] Liam: Redwood supports SAML SSO for admin/UI access and SCIM for provisioning. For API keys and service identities we support scoped service tokens and fine-grained roles. Audit logs include token-level usage so you can tie calls back to identities.
[44:00] Devon: regarding network topology — we run across multiple accounts for prod and non-prod. Can you integrate with a Transit Gateway pattern?
[45:10] Liam: yes, we support transit gateway or VPC peering across accounts. For multiregion we recommend transit gateway for simpler routing; peering is okay for single pair relationships. We'll include sample route tables in the diagram.
[47:30] Alicia: IDS/IPS and egress inspection — do you have any built-in WAF or IDS, or do you expect customers to place network inspection in front?
[48:15] Liam: typically customers place egress inspection/proxy and IDS in front of control plane endpoints. Redwood can optionally integrate with network TAPs and send telemetry to your IDS. For application-level protections, we do request-rate limiting, anomaly detection and can emit metrics to your observability stack.
[50:00] Marcus: service account key rotation — what are recommended rotation windows? Also how are long-lived tokens prevented?
[50:40] Liam: we recommend short-lived service tokens (hours) and automatic rotation for any long-lived keys. For user access we integrate with SSO and don't issue permanent passwords. We can provide tooling for automatic token rotation and vault integrations (HashiCorp Vault).
[52:20] Maya: small note on support SLA — for Dedicated/Private deployments we have enterprise SLA options and on-call support. We'll include our SLA and escalation matrix in the doc bundle.
[53:10] Devon: curious about on-prem option — if we deploy on-prem, what's the expected footprint and networking footprint?
[54:05] Liam: footprint varies by model and throughput. For a pilot we typically recommend a 4-GPU cluster (A100 or equivalent) for throughput testing; network-wise you need control plane access from admin hosts and connectivity to your KMS. We'll include a sizing guide.
[55:40] Alicia: ok, last items — we need to validate the legal security questionnaire and confirm any data residency requirements. We operate in NA and EMEA, some PII must stay in EMEA.
[56:30] Maya: understood — data residency is supported by pinning model storage and logs to region-specific buckets and running inference nodes in region. We'll document region-specific deployment options.
[58:10] Marcus: one small thing — we want proof that logs cannot be altered by Redwood. You mentioned signed logs and bucket policies; can you also show an example manifest?
[59:00] Liam: yes, we'll provide an example signed-log manifest and recommended S3 bucket policy that denies delete unless a specific multi-party role allows it.
[59:50] Maya: great — recap: Maya will share SOC2/ISO docs and pen test summary link; Liam will deliver detailed VPC diagram + port spreadsheet and signed-log manifest; Marcus/Devon will send KMS/HSM requirements and confirm peering method. We'll target pilot kickoff after diagram review. Thanks everyone.
